speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Some 12 years ago, I led a workgroup and tabled the Maintenance of Parents (Amendment) Bill 2010.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: After more than a decade, it was timely for another review.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I would also like to thank the members of the Alliance for Action to Strengthen Marriages and Family Relationships – in particular, Ms Hazlina, Dr Mathews, Ms Long Chey May, Mr Jasper Yap, Mr Abdul Karim, Mdm Zulaiha and Mr Arthur Ling – for their partnership with my workgroup in conducting the focus groups and survey, and in contributing their views on the amendments.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I would also like to thank members of public, partners and stakeholders who had given so much of their time to provide us with their views.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This includes more than 200 participants at our focus group discussions, over 1,000 survey respondents, and the people behind the responses to our public consultation paper.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The last key amendment in 2010 was to advocate for the "conciliation-first" approach.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This has been effective in reducing the number of cases that have to be put before the Tribunal for resolution.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The world has changed quite significantly in the last 12 years.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We have also learnt more about the way the Maintenance of Parents Act (MPA) works.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: So, having reviewed it, our Workgroup opine that it is time for more changes.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: At the same time, it is important to note what endures and will endure.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: My workgroup's recommendations are guided by the principles of the MPA.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: First is "family as the first line of support".

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The MPA is not intended to legislate or enforce filial piety, but to ensure that children provide for their needy elderly parents at a basic minimum level.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: MPA is a necessary last resort to provide legal recourse for neglected parents to get maintenance from their children for their basic needs.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: It respects the duty of an adult to his parents, and requires that each of us carry this duty, rather than pass it onto our fellowmen, in requiring that the state provides this private care.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The obligation imposed on children to maintain their parents is not an absolute one.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In circumstances where the parents had abandoned, abused or neglected their children, then it may not be just and equitable for them to be ordered to maintain their parent.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Here, where there is no private duty, there is a public one.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The survey, which is statistically representative of national demographic proportions, found that four in five agreed with the principle of reciprocity, that it is important for the children to repay the care received during childhood to their parents.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Similarly, seven in 10 agreed that children have an obligation to care for their elderly parents.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: These findings are consistent with other studies, such as those conducted by the Ministry of Social and Family Development (MSF), that the vast majority of Singaporeans hold strongly to family values and agree that it is their duty to take care of their parents regardless of their qualities and faults.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: However, we are also aware of the view held by some, that children did not ask to be born and therefore owe nothing to their parents.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: There is obviously a gap in the argument since the duty to care for one's parents does not arise from an exchange of promises – a baby cannot ask to be born, just as he cannot make a promise to care for his parents.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: My own position is that this duty exists as a social fact, from the existence and the living out of a family relationship, not from an exchange of promises.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: As a matter of public policy, I want to say that the Act remains as a pillar of our society's position on the role of the family in supporting one another.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: It serves as a signal to those children who neglect their needy parents who had previously cared for them, that the law holds them liable for maintenance.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This represents an even-handed recalibration for both parties.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We recommend four key amendments to achieve this vision.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: These amendments have been developed with careful deliberation and fine-tuned after many consultations with citizens, stakeholders and professionals from social and legal sectors.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The first round was conducted in January 2022.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We made changes to our proposals along the way, taking in the feedback from the first round of consultations.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: By the time we reached the second round, feedback was generally positive for all the amendments.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Over the years, Commissioner and Tribunal have observed cases of parents filing for maintenance claims against the children whom they had abandoned, abused or neglected.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This had caused severe and undue distress to their children and it violates the principle of reciprocity and fairness that I had outlined earlier.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We want to put in place processes to prevent those who had abandoned, abused or neglected their children from misusing the MPA and to spare their children from unnecessary distress.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: For abuse victims, the mere experience of going through the proceedings under the MPA can be distressing because it involves facing the parent after years of avoidance and recounting the experiences that they had tried to forget.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Indeed, the experience of the parent's abandonment, abuse or neglect has a serious impact on a person's life.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Research on adverse childhood experiences showed that even decades later, exposure to reminders of the original event can trigger severe reactions and adult survivors of child abuse may relieve their trauma almost as if the incident were occurring again.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I have talked to and I have listened to adults recounting their childhood experiences that their parent inflicted on them: it was painful and heartbreaking.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: For the cases that eventually came before the Tribunal for a hearing, the majority were dismissed as it was not just and equitable for maintenance to be granted.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Section 5(4) of the MPA currently provides for the Tribunal to dismiss any claim for maintenance or order a lower amount if it is satisfied upon due proof that the parent had abandoned, abused or neglected the child.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: However, having to go through the proceedings may have already caused significant distress and re-traumatisation to the person.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Some might even just have given in to the parent's demands for maintenance in order to avoid further distress.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Bella, not her real name, is in her late 20s and was subject to a maintenance application by her father.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: She had suffered from physical abuse and neglect from her father since she was a child.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: She and her mother had a personal protection order (PPO) against him after an incident which left her with injuries on her knee and her wrist.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The Tribunal dismissed the application in the end, but only after the proceedings which involved having to provide written accounts of the abuse.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: And then, there was a conciliation process, the mediation and a full hearing with all the parties.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Specifically, the new process would entail: One, parents to declare whether they had records of abuse, neglect or abandonment against the child whom they are claiming against.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Two, the Commissioner to screen against official databases for prescribed records of abandonment, abuse, or neglect.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: And examples of such records could include PPOs, Care and Protection Orders, Orders under the Vulnerable Adults Act, criminal convictions where the offence was committed against the child and investigation records from Protective Services under MSF.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Where records are present, Commissioner would refuse or terminate conciliation.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The parent would have to go before Tribunal for permission to proceed with the claim.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: If permission is granted and the case proceeds to a Tribunal hearing that includes the respondents, the Tribunal can still make a finding that the parent had abandoned, abused or neglected the respondent child based on the evidence as provided by the respondent and dismiss the case.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The general approach would be to not notify and involve the child in the hearing at this stage.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: A new section 3A will introduce a new requirement for the parent to declare at the time of making the claim, whether the parent has any record of abandonment, abuse or neglect of the child.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Section 14A(1) already allows the Tribunal and the Commissioner to obtain information, records, documents or articles from prescribed agencies for the purposes set out in subsection (2), which presently includes supplementing the information provided by the parties.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Subsection (2) will be expanded to enable the Tribunal and the Commissioner to obtain records to verify the truthfulness of the declaration made under new section 3A and to use these records to fairly determine the case.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Some of the information or documents might be subject to gag orders or statutory prohibitions against publication.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The amended section 14A(1A) will enable the Tribunal or the Commissioner to obtain these records but only for the purpose of ascertaining whether the parent has a record of abandonment, abuse or neglect of his or her child.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: These records will obviously have to be treated very carefully after they are obtained.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The other amendments to section 14A introduce special safeguards and protections for such information or documents.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We considered this and we too wish that this was possible.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: However, where there are no records in official databases, it is necessary for the child to be called upon to provide the accounts of abandonment, abuse or neglect, which would otherwise be unknown to the Tribunal.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Moreover, we have to balance between protecting the child and ensuring that the elderly parent have fair access to justice.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We need to be fair to both sides.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We hear the concerns and would like to assure Members in this House that the Tribunal and the Commissioner have trauma-informed practices in place to sensitively manage and to minimise distress to the children.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Our second amendment concerns the dismissal of frivolous or vexatious applications.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: When I reviewed the MPA in 2010, one of the key thrusts was to ensure that the administrative processes behind the Act are beneficiary-centric, so that any additional or unwarranted stress put on the families should be minimised.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: At that time, we proposed to give the President and Deputy President of the Tribunal powers to dismiss frivolous or vexatious applications under section 3 of the Act, that is, for "fresh" applications.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In the same spirit, and also recognising the distress that can be caused to children as a result of these proceedings, we are further enhancing the powers of dismissal for frivolous and vexatious applications.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Currently, the Tribunal has existing powers to dismiss variation applications under section 14(7)(a) of the Act, but a Tribunal quorum is reached only where there are three members present.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: And this can be done where it is already clear from the existing evidence that the application is without merit, for example, where the applicant is clearly financially able to maintain himself or the child clearly has no means to maintain the parent because he himself is receiving long-term financial assistance.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Another example would be the application is one that had been previously dismissed and there is no change in circumstances.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: One individual who participated in our second round of public consultations had raised the concern that improving the ease of dismissal would deter genuine applications.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The President and Deputy Presidents of the Tribunal, being experienced legal professionals, are well qualified to determine the merits of the case.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Here, the balance is between ensuring that the case is fully considered, with efficiency considerations.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: There is no doubt that the former is more important than the latter, but there is also no need for an overly onerous process which benefits neither party.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The amendments I have surfaced thus far aim to protect children from potential misuse of the MPA.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Under the Destitute Persons Act, destitute persons can be admitted into welfare homes if they are unable to support themselves and lack family support.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Before admission, family members are engaged and they are encouraged to care for the destitute person.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: However, representatives of welfare homes who attended our focus group discussions observed that there are destitute parents, albeit a small number, who have children with the means to maintain them but do not do so.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Although the MPA empowers such needy parents to claim maintenance from their children, they often choose not to, due to fears of further straining the relationship.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In some cases, the parents have lost contact with their children and the welfare homes are unable to locate or contact the children.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Despite repeated attempts at persuasion, the welfare homes are often unable to get the children to give maintenance or persuade the parent to apply for maintenance under the MPA.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In such cases, there is nothing the welfare homes nor the authorities can do to get the children to fulfil their obligations to the parent who had raised and cared for them.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: As a result, such children effectively leave their parents to the care of the state when they can well afford to maintain them.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This, in our opinion, is an unfair use of public funds.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Our initial proposal was to empower the Commissioner to apply for maintenance on behalf of such destitute parents, even without their consent.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: One-third of survey respondents were of the view that the parent's wishes should be respected.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This softer approach will still uphold the principle that children have the obligation to maintain their parents and allow the Commissioner to hear the children's side of the story and encourage the child to support the parent, where appropriate.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: To ensure that we do not unduly cause distress to the child, the Commissioner will only exercise this power where the Commissioner finds that the parent does not have any record of abandonment, abuse or neglect of the child.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The Commissioner, in exercising his current powers under the Act to identify and locate the child, will also assess his ability to maintain the parent using information from prescribed agencies under the current section 14A of the Act.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The Commissioner will only initiate conciliation proceedings if, from the information obtained, he reasonably believes that the child is able to provide maintenance for the destitute parent.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: It is in this sense limited to cases where the abandonment of the parent is especially egregious.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Maintenance cases before the Tribunal are often acrimonious and involve deep underlying issues that are not solved by only a monetary order.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Indeed, the Tribunal has observed cases where non-monetary directions could help to address fundamental issues in the family.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Addressing these issues will also go towards promoting the durability and sustainability of the maintenance order.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: One clear example is when the parent has issues with problem gambling.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Similarly, if the Tribunal finds that the children's complaints against the parent's behaviour is valid, it can require the parent to cease performing that act which causes harm or suffering to the children.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: And for highly acrimonious cases with underlying relational issues, family counselling is a potential order that can be made as well.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: With regard to enforcement, the Tribunal will be able to order that the maintenance payments that is due to the parent under an order of the Tribunal that they be withheld from the parent, until the parent complies with the non-monetary direction.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I am aware that this is a paradox – mending family ties requires us to go beyond money, but going beyond the ordering of maintenance leads down, some would say further down, the road to paternalism.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: It is indeed a road which I am reluctant to tread on, so I would like to say that this amendment is probably the furthest I would go in this direction and I would leave personal relationships to the personal realm.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: One individual wrote a Forum letter that counselling is not always enough to ensure a real change in the behaviour of a problem gambler.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We also had feedback from our public consultations that the child should not have to pay if the parent fulfils the counselling order but returns to gambling later on.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: If the parent returns to the same behaviour later on, the child can apply to the Tribunal for a variation of the maintenance order and the Tribunal can consider whether that is fair depending on the facts of the case.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Some options the Tribunal could take up would be to change the mode of payment, so that the child pays the maintenance not in cash but through direct payment in areas such as utilities, medical care or groceries.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: There may be cases where the Tribunal could make other directions such as stopping harassment or giving a child access to visit his parent.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The amendment will give the Tribunal more options to help and address the specific issues of the families involved in the claim.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Minors below the age of 21 remain under parental authority and control on a wide range of matters and so should not be subjected to the proceedings under this Act, which has always been intended to impose the obligation on adult children to support their parents.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: New section 12C makes conciliation proceedings confidential and disallow legal representation, similar to current Tribunal proceedings.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: New section 20A serves to protect conciliation officers and mediators from personal liability in carrying out their statutory functions, if they had acted in good faith and with reasonable care.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In closing, I wish to reiterate that the MPA is not about legislating filial piety.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The law is not the appropriate vehicle for inculcating family values.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The effort in promoting family values starts from families themselves, and flows out to schools, and the community and ethnic groups and voluntary welfare organisations (VWOs).

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I hope that as a society, we can continue to uphold family values of mutual support for each other.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: After all, the family is the basic building block of society.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The MPA is needed so that there is legal recourse for the needy elderly parents who struggle with unfilial children who refuse to support them.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: It also sends out a clear signal of what we as a society stand by.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I had said that I would leave personal relationships to the personal realm.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As hon Members know, it is not often that we get a chance to be directly involved in the conceptualisation and, if passed by this House, the passage of a Private Member's Bill.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The remit of the workgroup was to improve the workings of the Act and to ensure that it continues to be fit for purpose for the foreseeable future.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This Private Member's amendment Bill represents the culmination of a stupendous amount of work put in by the workgroup, its partners and stakeholders over the past two years.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Insofar as ideas for improvement were concerned, we started from a clean slate – meaning we looked at all aspects of the current law and its practice.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Together, we organised focus group discussions, ran surveys and issued a public consultation paper.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Through these platforms, we gathered public feedback on the Act, identified areas for improvement, brainstormed and formulated proposals that were then stress-tested with the participants and thereafter reviewed once again.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is heartening to note that many fellow Singaporeans from all walks of life stepped up to provide their valuable views at every stage of the consultation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This Bill is a testimony of the inputs and deliberations that the workgroup received in its distilled form.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It derives its strength from our collective ideas and our pursuit of common values, and the sense of justice for all parties.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As can be seen in the rest of my speech, these are not easy issues – to what extent is a person entitled to rely on his children for support, to what extent a person's freedom to use his own money as he sees fit, is constrained by his duty to his parent, and finally, to what extent is the state responsible for a man when even the most intimate ties of family fail?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I think it is also appropriate to pay tribute to the then hon Nominated Member of Parliament, Prof Walter Woon, who, almost three decades ago, in 1994, mooted the need for this House to legislate maintenance of parents by their children as a last resort in certain circumstances.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: When he tabled the Maintenance of Parents Bill, it generated some level of controversy in and outside the House.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Now, the policy underpinnings of the Maintenance of Parents Act are received as wisdom.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is a visionary piece of unsentimental legislation – one which spells out the obligations of a child to his parent, and more importantly, as we shall see today, the limits of such obligations.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: First, where the parent's declaration under section 3A states he has a record of ANA of the child.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Second, where the Commissioner notifies the person that the parent has a record or purported record of ANA.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is a consequence of the new requirement under clause 15 of the Bill that vest with the Commissioner the power to ascertain if the parent is believed to have a record of ANA of the child.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This screening requirement is independent of the declaration by the parent.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And third, where a conciliation officer discontinues any conciliation in respect of the child's maintenance of the parent upon noting that the parent has a record or purported record of ANA of the child.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Here, we are dealing with a scenario where the parent did not raise any record of ANA in his declaration and the Commissioner did not detect any record through his screening.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As a result, the matter would have headed to conciliation as per the current process.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is contemplated that the child may raise facts suggesting that the parent has a record of ANA.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Hence, we provided that the conciliation should stop in such circumstances and the parent should get permission from the Tribunal before it may resume.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In short, the parent, the Commissioner and the child are all possible sources of notice of ANA.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Under the proposed section 3(B)(3) in the Bill, the President or Deputy President may grant permission, but if he or she is of the view that there is a significant possibility that permission should not be granted, then a three-member quorum should be convened to make a decision, which can include the referring President or Deputy President.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The policy intent here is to allow the President or Deputy President the power to act singly to give permission for the parent in question to commence proceedings in straightforward cases.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: However, for cases where it is contemplated that permission will be refused, then a three-member Tribunal must be convened to make such a determination.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This measure will safeguard the parent's interest in ensuring that his case is adequately deliberated before a decision is made against him.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I now come to the important issue of threshold upon which the President, Deputy President or Tribunal will have to decide whether permission should be given.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is provided for in the proposed section 3B(7) in the Bill.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is because a record of ANA involves not just a matter of fact, which is dealt with at the first level, but a matter of degree, in respect of which the second level is meant to address.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: What is meant by a "good arguable case"?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: What this also means is that the decision of the Tribunal at this stage is not dispositive of the ultimate issue at the hearing, which is whether, under section 5 of the Act, it should make a maintenance order against child if it considers it just and equitable that the child should maintain the parent.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Tribunal's grant of permission under section 3B in the Bill is not intended to tie its hands in relation to its deliberation and decision on the ultimate issue.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Whether or not, as a matter of fact, the parent has abandoned, neglected or abused the child will continue to remain relevant at the hearing – relevant but not determinative.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is specifically provided for in the current section 5(4) of the Act.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I now move to the circumstances in which the child may be allowed to participate in proceedings on the application for permission.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As can be seen from the proposed section 3B(2) in the Bill, there is only a narrow exception to the rule that the child is not to be informed nor involved in the proceedings.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is because the policy objective is to prevent the child against whom the parent had a record of ANA from being subject to distress.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Where, however, in a situation where the application for permission is filed arising from the discontinuation of conciliation, where information of the parent's record of ANA surfaced, the child would already be informed of the parent's claim.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As I mentioned earlier, it is probable that the child would be the one who surfaces information pertaining to the parent's record of ANA.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Here, in these specific circumstances, it is provided that if the child so wishes, he will be informed and he may be involved in the proceedings.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This will enable him to lead evidence on matters pertaining to the parent's record of ANA that he surfaced at the conciliation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This must be so as a matter of fairness.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In the event the Tribunal gives permission to allow the parent to claim maintenance from the child, then under the proposed section 12A(4) in the Bill, the matter should be referred for conciliation as per the current process.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The current amendments are not meant to detract from the "conciliation-first approach" adopted by way of amendments to the Act in 2010.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Since 2010, conciliation has been proven to be more successful in addressing and resolving the core issues between the parties and also has resulted in the savings of significant time and resources.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I now deal with appeals against the decision of the Tribunal to the General Division of the High Court.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In addition, any appeal under the proposed section 18(3A) must satisfy the conditions in the current 18(2) of the Act, in that the appeal must involve a question of law or of mixed law and fact.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Otherwise, the decision of the Tribunal is final, as is the case now.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Also, unless the High Court directs otherwise, the appeal documents should not be served on the child.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The appeal is also to be heard and determined without informing or involving the child.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is again consonant with the aim of the Bill, which is to spare the child who has been subject of ANA by his parent the distress of being informed and involved in the appeal proceedings.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This position also applies in the situation where the child was originally informed and involved in the application for permission before the Tribunal.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The appellant's interest is nonetheless safeguarded since the High Court has powers to issue directions requiring the child to attend the hearing of the appeal in appropriate circumstances as it sees fit.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: How about cases where there are existing orders made in favour of parents even though they have records of ANA against their children?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As was mentioned by the hon Member Mr Seah in his speech, the sense is that in the past, there may have been cases where the children may have decided to just give in to their parents' demands for maintenance so as to avoid traumatisation and distress.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: So, what is the recourse for such children?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: They may make an application to rescind or vary the maintenance order on the basis that their parents have records of ANA.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: When such applications are made, the Tribunal, under the proposed section 14A in the Bill, will have powers to conduct screening against the parents and obtain the necessary information on the parents' records of ANA too.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is provided for under the proposed section 14A in the Bill.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Typically, the Court imposes gag orders in circumstances where it is necessary to protect identities of minors or victims of criminal offences, especially victims of sexual crimes.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There could be situations where gag orders are imposed, preventing the disclosure of information on the identity of accused persons because their identities can lead to the establishment of the identities of the victims.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is particularly so where the accused persons could be the victims' parents.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: On the other hand, there is a need for safeguards to be in place so that the rationale behind the imposition of the gag order is not thwarted.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In addition, there is a strict prohibition against disclosure to any other person save for the Commissioner, the Tribunal, the parent and the applicant for permission.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: However, these amendments provide us with not easy, but practical answers.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: They are a response to these questions which rests on our collective values.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I think it is worth spelling these out so that the policy intent is clear.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: First, that there remains a tie between a child and his parent, one which is born of the bare fact of the relationship rather than the quality of such relationships.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: That alone allows us a basis to consider cases as falling under this law.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This underlines the importance of the family in the Singapore context.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Second, such a tie, however, may or may not entail specific duties.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Here, the test is a purely negative one.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As long as the parent has not abused the child or treated him poorly, a duty is born.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Again, this makes no pretence about the quality of parenting as a requirement, merely the minimum providence of some basic needs for a child.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Third, and perhaps most importantly, this law does not circumscribe the Government's commitment to a citizen, which has a fairly neutral lens in relation to his parenting profile.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: That is to say, a man may be a terrible father but he is still a citizen and one does not have to be a good citizen – however this is defined – to benefit from the state's provision of resources towards one's welfare, which includes housing, healthcare, food and a certain quality of life.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I see this as a strength – that this law both limits the obligations of a child towards his abusive parent and spells out our obligations to each other as fellow citizens.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It has been a privilege to be part of the workgroup led by my hon colleague Mr Seah Kian Peng in reviewing the Act and engaging the public and key stakeholders during the process.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I join the hon Mr Seah in thanking the Action to Strengthen Marriages and Family Relationships, self-help groups, social workers, legal experts and fellow Singaporeans who have so generously shared their feedback and opinions with us.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Through the review, I have learnt much from the rich conversations we have had with the various stakeholder groups.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Given the extensive speeches by my hon colleague Mr Seah Kian Peng and Mr Murali Pillai earlier, allow me to speak in Mandarin.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: (In Mandarin):   Since young, my mother has taught me the importance of showing gratitude, and I have witnessed how my father took care of my grandmother after my grandfather's passing, until she passed away when she was 100 years old.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: So, I have always believed that the maintenance of parents is my responsibility.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: However, as I grew up, I realised that the world is actually very complex.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: For example, in Macpherson, where I have served for 12 years, I have come across lonely seniors who are neglected by their children.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Once, when I visited a block of rental flats, I met an elderly resident.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: She was very friendly, and she needed to buy a medicated patch for pain relief, so that she can walk, but was afraid that she could not afford it, and there was nobody to help her buy it.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We agreed to buy the patch for her, and she was very happy, genuinely happy.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: During our conversation, I learned that she has a daughter who has a good job and lives in a condo.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The resident was full of pride when she talked about her daughter.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But when we asked if her daughter visits her or takes care of her, she was unwilling to tell us more.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: After we left, I kept thinking about why her daughter lives in a condo, yet she was living in a rental flat?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Why is it so difficult to even buy a medicated patch?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Later on, I met another elderly resident who wanted to apply for maintenance from his children.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: He was rejected in his previous application, and he was very angry, and he wanted to reapply again years later.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Subsequently, I looked at the documents he brought and found out that he was jailed for some offences several years ago, and his children were brought up mainly by his wife.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: He was also suspected of molesting his daughter, so his children did not want to have anything to do with him.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Both residents face maintenance issues, but their situations are different, and it prompts us to think deeply about the issues.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Today, we debate the Maintenance of Parents (Amendment) Bill in Parliament.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This Act came into force in 1996, with the objective of helping seniors who do not have means to support their basic living expenses by providing a legal avenue for them to obtain maintenance from their children.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The amendments we are debating today aims to strengthen the existing mechanisms, so that seniors neglected by their children can be taken care of, while avoiding abuse of the Act to protect the interests of the offspring.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In 2010, amendments were introduced to incorporate mediation into the process, and results have been encouraging so far.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It has been more than a decade since the last amendment, with our ageing population and changes in the family structure, the current review and amendments bears significant meaning.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We found that some of these relationships soured because of certain reasons.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Therefore, the Commissioner or Tribunal should be further empowered or have greater flexibility to help these families reunite.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: These include seniors who are living in welfare homes or applying to live in one, according to the Destitute Persons Act.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: They may have fallen into destitution due to various reasons, but if they are responsible parents, then their contributions should be repaid.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This amendment Bill empowers the Commissioner, even without the agreement of the destitute elderly, the Commissioner can contact his/her children for mediation.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: If his/her children still refuse to pay maintenance, at least attempts to re-establish contact is made.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Currently, there are few seniors in this situation.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The workgroup initially considered the option for the Commissioner to apply for maintenance on the parents' behalf.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: After all, if the parents did take care of their children, and their children do have the means, they should pay for some living expenses.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: However, during public consultation, some members of the public are concerned that this will deprive the parents of their autonomy or may lead to greater hostility towards the parents on the part of the children.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Of course, the Commissioner must first assess if the parent did take on child-rearing responsibilities, and if his/her children do have the capacity to pay for maintenance.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In addition, some parents may have bad habits that cause family relations to sour.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: According to data from the Tribunal, around 10% of cases involve a parent with gambling problems.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: If he/she is non-compliant, then his/her children will not be obligated to pay maintenance.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Second conclusion, adult children who have been abused, neglected or abandoned by their parents should be better protected.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: During our consultations with experts and the public, we found that these children grow up to live seemingly normal lives, but they may not have put the trauma behind.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: When these children receive notices to demand for parent maintenance, some may go to Court.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Although they are able to prove that they have been harmed or their parents did not fulfil their child-rearing duties, the process will undoubtedly cause old scars to resurface.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Once, I witnessed a Court proceeding where a parent was applying for maintenance from the children.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Even though the daughter is now a mother, the sight of her parent was enough to induce fear, to the point that when the parent came near, she immediately ran away to hide, and was even trembling in fear.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It is clear that the trauma is still there.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Last year, a survey involving more than a thousand people also show that most Singaporeans agree that there is a need to protect people who have been abused, neglected or abandoned by their parents.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: And most agree that it is necessary to prevent their parents from obtaining maintenance.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: If there are such records, the applicant must prove that he/she had fulfilled child-rearing duties and must obtain approval from the Tribunal before applying for maintenance.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Without the Tribunal's approval, the affected offspring will not be notified.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: If there are no records of abuse, they will be notified, and the application will proceed as normal to be fair to both parties.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The third conclusion, the Act must help parents who have taken on child-rearing responsibilities but are in destitution due to neglect in their twilight years.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But the Act should not become a tool for parents to attack their children.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The Commissioner and Tribunal members observed that a minority of parents do not qualify to obtain maintenance.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: To ensure that this will not deter seniors in real need from applying, the amendment Bill stipulates that this only applies for applicants who do not fulfil the original conditions, or who are self-sufficient, where the children can show proof that they cannot afford to pay maintenance, or applicants who have been rejected by the Courts before.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I have just covered the key amendments of this Bill.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: During the review, the workgroup has actually considered a suggestion for grandparents to apply for maintenance.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I believe that fellow members have encountered situations during Meet-the-People Sessions (MPS), where the parents were absent, and children were brought up by their grandparents.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: For such cases, the grandparents who have brought up the child may deserve maintenance more, as they are older and have a harder time bring up the child.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: However, after public consultation, we believe that if we allow this, then we have to include other family members who have brought up the child too, for example, uncles, aunties, etc.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This requires further studies, so the workgroup decided not to adopt this suggestion.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In the long run, I think we need to consider how an ageing population and the increase in smaller families will impact the meaning of family in our future society, and how Asian traditional values will be affected.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: During MPS, I often meet seniors in financial difficulties approaching us for help.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: They struggle to pay for daily expenses but are unwilling to ask their children for help.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I once spoke to an elderly resident, who said her children are getting on quite well.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: When I asked if her children visit her or give her an allowance, she sadly replied that they have their own families.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: She said that bringing up children is a parental duty, if her children are filial, they will give her an allowance voluntarily and it will not be necessary for her to ask for it.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Obviously, deep inside, she hopes that her children will provide for her and show concern.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But maybe because of pride, or due to maternal love, she never asked for anything from her children and chose to suffer silently.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This is not the only case that I have seen.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As an Member of Parliament, we will definitely do our best to help them with their daily lives.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But I feel that if parents had genuinely cared for their children, then their children should provide some support.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Even if they are unable to pay for all the living expenses of their parents, they should shoulder some responsibilities.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: If not, what will become of filial piety?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Here, I would like to emphasise that filial piety does not mean that one should expect children to pay for their parents' living expenses regardless of circumstances.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: After considering the pros and cons, I believe the amendments will lead to a fairer legislation and ensure that deserving parents are protected.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I want to focus my speech on the issue of trauma-informed practices.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In recent rounds of public consultation, we have received feedback regarding cases where children alleged they were abused but whose cases had no official records as they went unreported.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We recognise the importance of recognising the trauma faced by these children, but we also acknowledge the need to ensure fairness and due process for the elderly parents who may face allegations without substantiated evidence.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Striking this balance is crucial to uphold our principles of justice and compassion.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In our pursuit of a solution, we have explored various avenues, and one key aspect we have delved into is the implementation of trauma-informed practices within the Tribunal and Commissioner.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Now, what exactly do we mean by trauma-informed practices?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Let us take a moment to understand this concept, as it forms an essential part of our approach.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Trauma-informed practices are an evidence-based framework that acknowledges the prevalence and impact of trauma on individuals' lives.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This approach recognises that children who have suffered abuse or neglect often bear the invisible scars of their experiences, which can significantly affect their emotional, psychological and social well-being.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: By adopting trauma-informed practices, we aim to create a supportive and safe environment for these children within the justice system.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: These practices involve training and educating the staff on trauma-sensitive approaches, ensuring they have the necessary skills and understanding to respond to the unique needs of children who may not have official records, and promoting collaboration between relevant agencies to protect all affected parties.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I want to emphasise that our commitment to trauma-informed practices does not absolve parents from their responsibilities.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We firmly believe that parents should be held accountable for their actions.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, through trauma-informed practices, we strive to strike a delicate balance, protecting the child while ensuring that the elderly parent also has fair access to justice.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As a fellow contributor to this amendment Bill, I would like to emphasise the enormous efforts we have made to guarantee a comprehensive and inclusive process.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We have meticulously conducted discussions and engagements, soliciting opinions and perspectives from a wide range of stakeholders.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: These efforts have aided in the development of the legislation under consideration today.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Several key issues were highlighted during these meetings, such as cases of grandparents requesting maintenance from their grandchildren.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: To safeguard the legislation's feasibility and legality, a line ought to be drawn.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While grandparents seeking maintenance from their grandchildren is a legitimate concern, extending their purview to include such claims may result in an inundation of claims from other members of the extended family.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This might make the legislation's execution and enforcement more difficult, burdening the system and causing undue hardship on families.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We have covered a wide variety of viewpoints and taken into account the different demands of persons affected by the law during the consultation process.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While we must accept the limits that we may still face today even with the amendments to the Bill, our objective is to build a framework that is fair, practical and effective.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The decision to draw a line in this case illustrates our commitment to preserving clarity and making the legislation as effective and viable as possible for all parties concerned.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In Mandarin):   As one of the members participating in this amendment, I would like to emphasise, that we have made great efforts in the process to ensure comprehensiveness and inclusiveness.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We seriously discussed and engage with the public, asked for their opinions and perspectives.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The discussion process highlighted several key issues, among them is whether grandparents can claim maintenance from grandchildren.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is reasonable but to expand the scope of the claims under the Bill may result in claims from other members of extended families.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In English): Mdm Deputy Speaker, I conclude with my support for the Bill.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: After all, if someone is still nursing or hurting from the hurts and the wounds of childhood ill-treatment by their parents of neglect or abandonment, the last thing he or she needs is to go through any process that suggests that they are being unfilial.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: In the initial stages of developing this amendment, I had one concern for the children who may not have reported the incidents of abuse or neglect and hence, do not have records within the state system.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Given that many cases of domestic abuse or neglect still go unreported now despite increased awareness and education efforts in recent years, we must assume that, in the past, there are likely many cases of abuse or neglect that have gone unreported and recourse therefore must be provided for children who have suffered ill-treatment by their parents.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I am glad that amendment one, as proposed in its current version, still allows for respondents to present evidence to the Tribunal and have the case dismissed.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: While some may argue that for someone who has been abused before, to be approached to present evidence can itself be an experience that opens old wounds and be stressful and we should avoid that altogether, it is, unfortunately, something we cannot avoid.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: In this matter, I fall back on my own knowledge and experience as a transformation and healing coach, having worked with many adults to process and heal from their emotional and childhood wounds.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I am assured myself, having witnessed and facilitated many on their healing journeys, to give the public the same assurance, that not all "reminders of past bad experiences" are harmful.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: In fact, for true healing to take place, one often needs to confront the negative experiences of the past in order to see it through a new and empowered set of lens for our hearts to heal.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Whilst I understand the preference of many to avoid dredging up "old skeletons in a closet", I also know that with good therapeutic support in place, it can catalyse an important and liberating healing process that has long been put off.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I hope that the Ministry will continuously look into adequate resourcing to ensure this support is there.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: My initial reaction to this amendment when it was first raised in our workgroup was one of like "Really?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Do we really want to allow the state to request maintenance from children without the consent of the parent?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Is this something that we really want to step in on?" I am born in the 1980s.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I belong to the millennial generation and I am probably one of many from my generation who hold the following attitude.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Whilst many of us believe in filial piety and that it is a right thing to do to provide for and care for our parents when they are old, we do not place the same expectations on our children to do the same.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: The old Chinese saying "养儿防老" is commonly a phrase I used to hear from my mom and other adults around me as I was growing up.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I remember feeling rather disturbed as a child and a teenager hearing this; and sometimes, it made me wonder if the value of "me" was just to be an insurance for my parents when they grow old.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: It did not help with building up a strong sense of self-worth and it made me doubt if my parents really do love me for who I am. "Love" at that time felt rather transactional.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I am not ashamed to admit those were my thoughts as I was growing up.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: And I believe there could be youths and teenagers out there today who may wonder about this at times too.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Do my parents love me only because I do well in school and make them look good and because they need someone to look after them when they are old?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I have a friend, grown up, who recently got married and she is deliberating about whether to have a child.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: She has gone to have her eggs frozen but has not yet made a decision.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: When we talk about it amongst our women friends, she speaks about having a child as an "investment".

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: When we hear people around us talk about having children in those terms, we cannot help but wonder if even parental love is conditional.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: On top of that, there are various values that were taught to us as kids.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: The Chinese talks about filial piety; Malays have "ketaatan kepada ibu bapa" and our Indian friends probably have something equivalent.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: To a young person, "being filial" can feel like a set of obligations we must adhere to in order to be seen as a "good person".

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: In this way, love can feel like a duty, smelling distastefully to some like "obligation".

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: During one of the public consultations I attended, a young person expressed this: "The child did not ask to be born.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Why do adults make these decisions and then impose these obligations on their kids?" I was a little shocked.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: It was a provocative statement, but also valid.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Perhaps, I am the idealistic sort, pursuing an ideal notion of love, for it to be unconditional and without obligation, to be given freely and reciprocated if the recipient feels so moved to reciprocate.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: It will be nice if my children want to contribute to my maintenance when they grow up and I grow old, but it is also all right if they do not.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Is maintaining parents really something we want the Government to intervene on or to mandate?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I am very grateful that Mr Seah Kian Peng invited me to be a part of this workgroup proposing these amendments, for it helped me to understand these issues more deeply and to gain perspectives beyond my own.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Through the many rounds of discussions we had with fellow workgroup members, the Commissioner, members of the Tribunal and the focus group consultations we had with the public, I began to discover that my personal idealism for "unconditional love" is indeed just an ideal and not very practical when we consider what it means for the larger society, especially if one is not in a comfortable financial position to afford such idealism, such as the old and frail ones staying in their destitute homes, unfortunately finding themselves relying on state subvention to upkeep their remaining days.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I realised that this matter is not about whether the state is so stingy that it is unwilling to support the upkeep of those who are vulnerable and destitute, but a matter of "fairness" that needs to be addressed because a government is a steward of public resources that come from the people, to be used for the people.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: The question of "fairness" is a valid and legitimate one for many citizens who have a stake in how the finite resources of a country should be used.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Often, I hear resentment from loving people, giving people, the volunteers at our many charity distribution activities, when they see elderly residents come and take a ration goodie bag or a goodie bag or a bag of rice.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: And then, they see the same elderly folk being driven around by their children in expensive cars around the neighbourhood.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: They wonder and sometimes they grumble out loud, "These elderly do not need.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Then, someone else who needs this more is deprived of it." And indeed, this question is asked not because charitable hearted people are being stingy or calculative, but because with finite resources, someone else's well-being could be the opportunity cost of over-generosity.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: In my role as Member of Parliament whom residents come to for help, I have seen how despite the old Chinese adage of "养儿防老", which is having children to safeguard one's old age, what I saw in reality is that many elderly parents prefer not to impose this burden on their children, often when their children have the means to support them and especially so when their children do not have the means.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Others will ask about financial support from the Government when they are experiencing financial hardship, preferring to apply for welfare support, rather than to ask for their children's support.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: In many cases, parents are caught in a "give and give" mindset.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: They hardly ever want to take from their children.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: These encounters showed me that in many cases, parental love does not ask for returns.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: And whilst the idealist in me delights in observing such unconditional love, the pragmatist in me, wearing the hat of a steward of public resources feels torn.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: It is not an easy thing for the Government to have to balance.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Do we respect the elderly parents' wishes who do not want to approach their children, or do we go ahead and claim, in consideration of fairness in the allocation of resources?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: It is fortunate that the workgroup, upon discussion with the members of the public, were able to come up with a "win-win" solution that I felt comfortable and satisfied with.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I am also thankful for Chairman Mr Seah Kian Peng's empathy and openness even as he passionately leads the charge on this Bill, to allow for alternative approaches to the original proposal, so that we get to balance.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: This helps to achieve the balance needed, for fairness to fellow Singaporeans and also respects the relationship priority of the elderly parent.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Deputy Speaker, I rise in strong support of the amendments to the Maintenance of Parents (Amendment) Bill.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I have had the privilege of being part of the private Member's workgroup led by hon Member Seah Kian Peng, my long-time partner in service, like 13 years old, 2010 and now, in 2023.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: First, the history of the Maintenance of Parents Act, or MPA.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The MPA, which was passed in 1995, was the brainchild of ex-Nominated Member of Parliament, Prof Walter Woon.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It was a significant step forward in recognising the social responsibility of adult children to care for and support their parents who are financially dependent or vulnerable.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The MPA was last amended in 2010 to enhance its effectiveness.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: One of the pivotal provisions which was introduced then was that of conciliation before parents could file for maintenance orders.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Two key developments have come to light, which is why this latest review of the MPA is conducted.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: This situation not only causes trauma to the adult children but also raises the question on whether it is fair to obligate them to provide maintenance to parents who have mistreated them.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We feel that such behaviour is unacceptable and calls for correction.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: One, is the MPA still relevant in Singapore society today?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Two, can matters of familial relations be addressed through legal provisions?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: And three, can the MPA address the issue of retirement inadequacy for elderly parents in need?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Question one - is the MPA still relevant in Singapore society today?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Supporters of the Act argue that it reflects the enduring value of filial piety deeply rooted in our Singaporean culture.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: They believe that adult children have a social responsibility to care for and to support their parents, especially when parents are financially dependent or vulnerable or needy.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: These proponents contend that placing this responsibility on children prevents burdening the public welfare system, which is funded by other taxpayers.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: On the other hand, opponents of the Act emphasise the importance of individual choice and agency.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: They argue that adult children should have the freedom to decide whether or not they want to provide financial support to their needy parents.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Some even highlight that while parents choose to give birth to their children, the children themselves did not ask to be born.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Others then contend that they are already financially supporting their own families and have their own expenditures to cover, and should not be legally obligated to support their parents.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: But what does the current landscape inform us?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: An MSF report published in 2022 is called "Ageing Families in Singapore, 2010-2020".

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: This report highlights that families remain a key source of physical, emotional and financial support for the elderly.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: A majority of elderly individuals aged 65 years and above cited that they could rely on their married children, 90%, and unmarried children, 83% of them, for financial support in times of need.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Additionally, the 2018 the Housing and Development Board (HDB) Sample Household Survey reveals that 74% of HDB residents aged 55 and above received regular financial support from their children in 2018, a five-percentage point drop from 79% 10 years ago in 2008.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Nevertheless, expectations of filial piety – as very articulately explained or described by Ms Carrie Tan, my hon Member friend – expectations of filial piety norms are shifting across generations.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: My young adult friends remind me that there are alternative ways to express filial piety beyond solely financial support, such as paying for dinner outings, birthday gifts or spending family time together.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: This evolving trend suggests the need for each generation to plan for their own well-being to avoid over-reliance on their children.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: However, changes in society norms take time to fully materialise.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: While the landscape continues to shift, the MPA which obliges children to provide basic support to their parents in need, remains, in my mind, still relevant.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It acknowledges the possibility that without legal intervention, some elderly parents may face challenges in receiving the necessary care and support from their adult children.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It, therefore, serves as a safety net to ensure the well-being of these elderly parents.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Question two – can matters in familial relations be addressed through legal provisions?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Family dynamics and circumstances vary greatly from one family to another; and so it is important to acknowledge the limitations of the legal system in resolving familial conflicts and dynamics.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In one case, a woman – she is a professional executive – had a physically and verbally abusive father who had caused her immense trauma since young.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: This woman, who wrote in to me and Member Seah Kian Peng, spent many years of her life, 40 years, running away from the father, even to the extent of changing her legal name and at one time, living overseas to escape his threats.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The father stalked her and even resorted to social media to threaten her.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: To this day, this woman is still receiving medical treatment.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: When he filed a claim for maintenance from her, she pleaded to the Ministry to protect her identity and whereabouts.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: This case highlights the challenges of enforcing legal provisions when issues of abuse and safety are concerned.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Furthermore, in other cases, even when faced with similar circumstances, family members also can respond differently.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: At a Tribunal session I sat in to observe as a workgroup member, a pair of adult siblings responded quite differently to their mother whom they claim had abused them when young.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The brother chose to forgive the mother, while acknowledging her shortcomings.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The sister was re-traumatised, being even in the same room as the mother and shared that she is now seeing a counsellor again.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: And then, in other families, there are parents who refuse to file claims against their errant, able children for financial support, even when they are abandoned or neglected in eldercare facilities.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: These variations in responses in families just show the complexity of family relationships and the need for individualised approach; not cookie-cutter solutions.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The work of the Commissioner and Tribunal in conciliation and in issuing directives, is complex and challenging.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The provisions in this Bill that grant more flexibility and space for them to consider and conclude are, therefore, very essential.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Hence, I fully support any provisions in the Bill to grant more flexibility and space for the Commissioner and the Tribunal to consider and conclude.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It is, therefore, unlikely that family allowances alone will be the main source of elderly support, whether or not they are covered by the MPA.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Hence, the Act will not totally address the issue of retirement inadequacy for elderly parents in need.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Unfortunately, though, many Singaporeans are still unprepared for retirement.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: To address this, more proactive education should be in place so that every Singaporean has a clearer idea of their own Individual Retirement Adequacy Plan, and to also have their own Retirement Adequacy Plan.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The MPA then, is just one of the tools available for a small target group of seniors within the broader framework of retirement adequacy planning measures for Singapore's elderly.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: For instance, what if documented records of abuse or neglect are not available?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: How do we handle cases of children based overseas who refuse to comply?
