speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: And what if non-monetary measures directed by the Tribunal, such as family counseling, do not yield positive results?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: These are questions we will continue to have to ponder over.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Nevertheless, the principles of family being one's first stop for support, reciprocity and filial piety that is enshrined in the MPA are still worth retaining.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It is crucial for us legislators to stay vigilant about ageing trends, evolving expectations of parents and children, and to also draw lessons from other legislations.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: This will ensure the relevancy of the MPA and protect the well-being of our elderly through a balance of legal obligations and evolving cultural norms.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: With these considerations in mind, Madam, I wholeheartedly support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This amendment Bill has sparked discussions about the changing social dynamics in our society.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We are compelled to question the extent of financial responsibility that children should bear toward their parents as we navigate through the complexities of a rapidly ageing population and evolving family structures.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: With increasing life expectancies, how can children support their parents through a longer period of old age, even as they strive to provide for their families and their own retirement, is becoming an issue of concern.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We must find a delicate balance that upholds our cultural values while addressing the financial realities faced by families today.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How can we instil in our children from a young age the values of responsibility and care for their elders, the moral aspects of a good citizen "好公民"?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In Mandarin):   The Chinese saying "caring for the elderly and the young as if they are our own parents and children" reflects our values of filial piety and collective responsibility in Chinese culture.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Life is, in itself, a cycle, our parents pushed our strollers when we are infants, we push our parents in their wheelchairs when they are aged and sick.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In English): There is a traditional Chinese saying about caring for the elderly and the young as if they are our own parents and children, which reflects the values of filial piety and collective responsibility in Chinese culture.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Our parents pushed our strollers when we were infants.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We push our parents on their wheelchairs when they are aged and sick.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I advocate for leveraging the Ministry of Education (MOE)'s curriculum to incorporate the teachings on the importance of filial piety and the moral aspects of being good citizens.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: By integrating these values into our educational framework, we can nurture a sense of social responsibility and compassion in our younger generations.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I propose an integrated curriculum where MOE can work with relevant stakeholders to include teachings on filial piety and family values into a variety of disciplines, at various grade levels.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This strategy guarantees that students obtain a well-rounded education that emphasises vital moral and social ideals.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Education should be made holistic, in addition to academic courses, the curriculum should include character and citizenship education.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We can cultivate well-rounded individuals who appreciate the need of helping their parents as they age by adding teachings on empathy, respect and responsibility toward family and elders.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Education plays a pivotal role in shaping the moral compass of our society.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: By embedding the principles of filial piety and family values into our curriculum, we can promote an understanding of the significance of caring for our parents and elders.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Through age-appropriate lessons, children can be taught the value of financial planning, the challenges of aging and the importance of supporting their parents in their later years.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Additionally, we must acknowledge the importance of community engagement and support systems.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is not solely the responsibility of children to shoulder the financial burden alone.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: By fostering a sense of community care and establishing support networks, we can share the responsibility and ensure that no family or child is overwhelmed by the financial obligations of supporting ageing parents.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Furthermore, we should encourage open dialogues amongst family members to discuss their financial situations, expectations and concerns.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This transparency can foster understanding, empathy, and a shared commitment among siblings to provide support according to their means.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: What happens if a parent had supported the child for a number of years before moving out of the child's life?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In some relationships, the interactions might be a combination of both care provision and abuse, or partial care and financial support in some years followed by abandonment or neglect in other years for a variety of reasons, such as conflict with the other parent, family problems, health or mental illnesses, and so on and so forth.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Another question I have is regarding the child from whom the parent seeks support.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: What if the parent has a few children but only seeks support from a particular one?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For example, the parent may choose to ask only – may only ask help from a child who happens to be unmarried with no children of his own.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: With or without children, everyone has an equal responsibility to support his or her parents.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I believe in taking a proactive approach by working with MOE to integrate teachings on filial piety and family values into our educational system.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: By nurturing a sense of responsibility and care for our elders, we can shape a society where the financial responsibility towards parents is shared, while upholding our cultural values.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Let us engage in meaningful discussions, seeking input from all segments of society, to craft a legislation that respects our traditions, recognises the evolving nature of our families, and ensures a fair distribution of financial responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It will also empower a Tribunal to better deal with frivolous or vexatious applications.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Bill will also allow the Commissioner and Tribunal to engage children of destitute parents and to facilitate conciliation where appropriate.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I left my speech on my chair and I think Member of Parliament Murali Pillai must have read it because he has addressed most of the points that I am about to raise but he said it, he felt that the points were pertinent ones, and he has foreseen that someone will raise it and that he will address it earlier on in this debate.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Under the new section 3B(2), the application for permission must be dealt with without informing or involving the child, except where the child was already involved in any prior conciliation and is agreeable to participate in proceedings.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I understand the need to avoid re-traumatising a child who may have been previously abandoned, abused or neglected, as Member of Parliament Murali had raised.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, the child may wish to have the opportunity to decide whether or not to participate in the application for permission.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Commissioner or Tribunal may grant permission for a maintenance application if they find that there is a good arguable case that the parent did not abandon, abuse or neglect the child.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Or there is a good arguable case that the child should maintain the parent on just and equitable ground.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: How can the Commissioner or Tribunal determine whether there is a good arguable case if the child does not even know that the application for permission has been made?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Has the Member considered whether it might be traumatic as well for a child who was not involved in the permission application to suddenly be told that he or she now face a maintenance application because the Commissioner or Tribunal found that there was no abandonment, abuse or neglect?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: And this finding was made without hearing from the child?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: How will the communication to the child be managed in this case?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: All the more so if the Tribunal found that there was a good arguable case that there was no abuse.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Member further share the rationale behind not even informing the child of the application for permission?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second set of clarifications is about allowing applications for permission where there are records of abandonment, abuse or neglect.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Member Murali had addressed my clarification on when the application for permission would be granted at the President or Deputy President and when it would be referred to the Tribunal for decision.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Beyond that, under the new section 3B(7), permission may be granted if there is a good arguable case that the parent did not abandon, abuse or neglect the child or that the child should maintain the parent on just and equitable grounds.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Member clarify what is required evidentially to show a good arguable case?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Given that suffering and abuse are contextual and subjective, can the Member share what guidance will be provided to the Tribunal to ensure consistency in decision-making?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Member also share if a child will have the opportunity to challenge the Tribunal's decision to grant permission for the maintenance application?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Lastly, my last clarification is on the definition of record or purported record of abandonment, abuse or neglect.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is defined as any record against or relating to the person that is prescribed to be a record or purported record of the person's abandonment, abuse or neglect of a child of the person.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, we are aware that there is a potential problem of underreported child abuse cases.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: MSF's data showed a sharp increase in child abuse cases over the past decade.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: MSF stated that this helped to sharpen the ability of sector professionals to pick up safety concerns for a child and seek appropriate intervention.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am glad that we are now investigating and detecting more abuse cases.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, this also suggests that there may have been a significant extent of under-reporting of child abuse prior to 2015.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: When our parents fall into needs, most of us would naturally want to help them and fulfil our filial piety duties.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: When parents take the responsibility of bringing up their children well, most will agree that it is right for their children to take care of them when they are no longer able to support themselves.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, where parents have abused or neglected their children when they were young, and subsequently seek maintenance support when their children become adults, this may lead to significant distress and re-traumatisation of childhood abuse or neglect during the maintenance claim process.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am privileged to be part of the workgroup led by the hon Mr Seah Kian Peng and my Parliamentary colleagues have shared extensively on how distressing emotionally and mentally it can be for adult children to be reminded of the abuse and neglect experienced when they were young and how the amendments will help to protect the abused victims with a fair process.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In the process of the workgroup review, we were brought to understanding several cases such as one where a mother had problem gambling behaviours and her son opposed the application, citing her gambling habits as the reason.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The application was dismissed and the Tribunal encouraged her to attend counselling.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As this was not mandatory, the mother only attended one session and the relationship between her and her children remain broken.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For cases that involve behavioural issues like problem gambling, alcoholism or drug addiction, adult children are often reluctant to pay maintenance as they are concerned that their parents would waste the money, entrench their problematic behaviours further and result in a worser outcomes than when they did not have the money.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Tribunal also shared that they often encounter families having deep-seeded conflicts and complex family issues that needed more professional intervention such as counselling.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Without addressing the underlying factors that cause a deep strain between parents and adult children, even if maintenance support is approved, non-compliance after a period will rise due to loss of trust and further breakdown in the relationships.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: When addressing such cases, there needs to be non-monetary orders especially professional interventions, beyond just addressing the living expenses through maintenance payments.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Professional counsellors or social workers can help the parents and adult children better understand the underlying problems and deal with root causes.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Currently, the Tribunal is only empowered to make orders on maintenance payments for the purpose of defraying the costs and expenses of the parent.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Counselling can provide a safe space and facilitate process for both parents and children to express their emotions and concerns.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For elderly parents struggling with addictions like gambling, counselling can allow them to discuss their challenges, and the underlying issues that contribute to their behaviour in a neutral setting, a support that they might not have had access to in the past.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Uncovering root causes of addictions and bad habits, which are often associated with deeper emotional or psychological issues such as stress, depression, loneliness, or a desire for excitement, is important for a conciliatory approach, to help develop healthier coping mechanisms.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Through mandatory counselling, elderly parents can learn effective coping strategies to deal with the triggers that lead to their addictions or bad habits, which strain family relationships, leading to conflicts, trust issues and financial problems.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Counselling can rebuild trust, establish healthy boundaries, enable forgiveness and foster a supportive environment for recovery.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The intent of this amendment is not for adult children to avoid maintenance payments but to ensure that the root cause of the problem that leads to adult children not maintaining their parents can be addressed holistically.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The aim is to benefit both parents and adult children to bring about better outcomes and resolutions.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In Mandarin):   Deputy Speaker, the Maintenance of Parents (Amendment) Bill tabled by the workgroup aims to formulate measures to protect children from abuse, neglect or abandonment and to prevent parents from abusing the laws and disturbing their children's lives and mind unnecessarily.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In my English speech, I mentioned a case whereby a mother with gambling addiction applied for maintenance from an adult child.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Although her application was rejected and the Tribunal also recommended that the mother undergo counselling, the mother did not continue after one visit.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This will also make future conciliation between the two sides difficult.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The workgroup believes that through counselling, the root of the problem can be addressed.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It can help addicted parents get rid of their addiction and repair family ties effectively.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In English): Mdm Deputy Speaker, as I conclude my speech, I would like to again express my gratitude to the leadership of Mr Seah Kian Peng as well as the teamwork from the workgroup that has done this review of the Maintenance of Parents Act and make the tabling of the amendment Bill today possible.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I would also like to thank members of the public as well as key stakeholders for raising their feedback and concerns through Focus Group Discussions, surveys and REACH consultation.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This Act was last amended in 2010 and, during these past 12 years, we have gained more experiences and insights on the operationalisation of the MPA.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Before I start, I declare my interest as a member of the Government Parliamentary Committee (GPC) for Social and Family Development and that I was part of the workgroup that helped to review the MPA.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Members of the workgroup have spoken on why they support the proposed provisions and my speech today will touch on why I think it is of utmost importance that we ensure that the MPA remains relevant.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Especially as my constituency, Radin Mas, has many seniors and I interact with many of them on an almost daily basis.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Occasionally, my grassroots leaders and I would come across cases where a senior would seek financial assistance and other means of assistance, as they were not adequately taken care of by their family members.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In such cases, we rely on the MPA as an avenue of last resort to provide a legal recourse for neglected seniors to receive a basic maintenance, in terms of financial support, from their children.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The responsibility of caring for our seniors must fundamentally lie first with the family.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The Government can support with broad-based financial and social support but the Government can only do so much.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: With Singapore on the path of becoming a super-aged society, where more than 20% of our population are 65 years old and above, it is timely that we review the MPA to ensure that this legal avenue of last resort remains effective.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This is particularly important in cases where the parent has lost touch with their children, or in cases where the destitute parent is unwilling to contact the children for fear of further straining the relationships.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: As the hon Member Mr Seah Kian Peng mentioned in his speech, the workgroup had initially wanted to empower the Commissioner to apply to the Tribunal for a Maintenance Order for the destitute parent, even if the parent did not provide consent.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This would allow us to ensure that financially able children would fulfil their obligation to maintain their parents.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: However, during the public consultation process, we received significant feedback that the wishes of the parent should be respected.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The Bill now takes a more balanced approach, where the Commissioner is empowered to locate the children of destitute parents and require them to attend conciliation so as to hear the children's side of the story.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I believe that this is a good balance as it enhances the chances of conciliation between parties.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: As the proportion of seniors in our society increases, we should do all we can to try to mend relationships, so that our elders can have the fullest support from their children as they age.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Loosely translated, it means that every family inevitably have their problems and issues.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: There have been cases where the children refuse to pay maintenance for their parents due to certain underlying issues.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In the past year, I have attended some of the Tribunal's hearings as an observer as part of the workgroup.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: One common argument put forth by the children was the physical abuse they had suffered under the parent when they were young.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Another common argument was the parent's serious gambling addiction, which often led to unresolved debts.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: So, no matter how much money is given to the parent, it is always "钱不够用" or "money not enough".

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Currently, the Tribunal is only empowered to make orders on maintenance payments and does not have legal standing to address and help resolve some of these underlying, non-monetary issues.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I fully support this, as it would help to address squarely some of the underlying reasons why certain parent-child relationships had deteriorated in some of these cases.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: As Singapore ages rapidly, we are likely to see more of such cases with issues potentially becoming increasingly complicated.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The proposed amendments in this Bill are timely and necessary but would certainly not be the last.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We must continue to review the Act periodically to ensure its effectiveness and relevance.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Indeed, the spirit of the Act in this amendment Bill is aligned around the clear axis and that is to create clear, protective safety nets for seniors and our vulnerable when their families fail them.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I welcome the updates and amendments to the Act, an Act which has served many vulnerable families well for the past three decades.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Given the pressures placed on families during COVID-19 and the many parent-children "break-ups" I have witnessed in my constituency, it is timely that we look to expanding the Maintenance Bill to include more downstream safety nets for conciliation and the continued transformation of the Maintenance Act into a platform for trust and reciprocity.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is easy to get along when you are meet each other once in a while, but it can be hard if you have to live together.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: During COVID-19, I met with quite a number of troubled seniors and their family members who have found it impossible to get along.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While each case was unique, the circumstances to how the situation developed to be so ran similar invariable scripts.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Child asks Mom and Dad to sell their current home to help fund the child's new marital home.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Parents oblige and even gift their life savings to Child.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Child promises to look after Parents into their golden years.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Fast forward a few years, living together brought much heartache to all parties involved.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Parents decide to move out but realise their very limited options given that they have no more savings or assets.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: She has three married children – a son and two daughters.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: She stays with her son and his family and has very, very strained relations with her daughter-in-law who suffers from suspected Obsessive Compulsive Disorder (OCD).

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In order to avoid her daughter-in-law for fear of putting her son in a difficult position, Mdm L wakes up at 3.00 am in the morning and is out of the house by 4.00 am.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: She sits by herself at the Seniors Corner for hours until 8.00 am, after which she leaves for her daughter's home to look after her two grandchildren.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: She returns home close to 10.00 pm after her daughter-in-law has returned back to her room.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Her children have all come to see me and tell me that they are unable to house Mdm L for various reasons.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Rental is her only option, but she does not qualify as her children are home owners and have viable careers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: They are technically able to look after their mother.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In the meantime, as she awaits her rental appeal, Mdm L's 3.00 am, 4.00 am, 8.00 am life runs like a nightmare Groundhog Day.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Another resident, Mdm C, a widow in her 80s, came home one day to find that her son had changed the locks to their home and her belongings left outside of her home.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: When she confronted her son about the matter, he said that his new wife could not bear living with her and he would like her out of the home; the home which she and her late husband had bought together for their son after selling their own home.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Having no place to go and no savings, Mdm C sought refuge with her daughter and together, they came to see me at our pro-bono legal clinic service.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Despite receiving advice that she should file a maintenance order against her son, Mdm C hesitated on doing so as she felt that she could not bear the shame of putting her son through a tribunal Court.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Like many before them, for both Mdm L and Mdm C, the 2011 expanded amendment to include a conciliation process with a trained and neutral mediator could have been a useful step in alleviating the vulnerable situation both parties found themselves in.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For Mdm L, a conciliation process could have bettered the relationship between her daughter-in-law and herself.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Given that issues typically centre around finances and housing, could we also consider the following to strengthen the conciliation process?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Could we also allow the conciliation platform to introduce such remedies, albeit conciliation not being a tribunal, being short of an order?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In the spirit of reciprocity, the introduction of such remedies could also extend to children and whole family facing such issues.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Over the years, the Maintenance Act has changed the trajectory of life for many of our vulnerable parents and with the upcoming amendments, it will seek to protect an even expanded group of vulnerables.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: In Singapore, the family is the bedrock of our society and the basic principle is that parents bring up children in a loving and positive family environment and the children, when they grow up, are responsible for supporting their parents.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: This principle stands on the value system of filial piety, which Asian societies hold dear, which Singapore holds dear, and which is universal across multicultural, multi-religious Singapore.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The different faiths practised here promote the same regard that children need to have for their parents through to their old age as long as they both are living.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: All also teach the same about how parents ought to treat their children and bring them up in a positive, loving family environment, providing and caring for them in their growing years until they are economically independent.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: For Singaporeans, filial piety is a value which have seen us grow and prosper in the past six decades since Independence and has been part of the foundation of our families and our society for continued happiness, prosperity and progress for our nation.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Most of us would recall the ritual of handing over a percentage of our pay cheque – later on, GIRO standing order – to our parents as part of our contribution to household expenses and for the maintenance of their well-being when we started our first job.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: It is a moment of pride, both for the child who has come of age and is independently earning a salary after years of depending on the parents for everything, almost, and for the parents who have arrived at a milestone of parenthood.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: This practice is a visible sign of filial piety and of the universal value of "honouring your father and your mother" that is practised across religious beliefs and traditions of the way of life such as Confucianism.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Financial contribution is but one way to practise filial piety.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Even more important is the practice of giving time to accompany our parents, to listen to their stories, to share with them our aspirations, to show them care and concern and to journey with them as they age.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: And if God willing, the parents may live to a ripe old age, blessing the next generations with their wisdom and sage.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: But alas, in a world with shifting values, legislation like the Maintenance of Parents Bill had to be put in place to protect the elderly parents from being abandoned by their children.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: It is equally unfortunate that there are cases where the parents have treated the child or children badly and have abused their children or even abandoned them, leaving the children to grow up with traumatic, deeply wounded experiences in their childhood.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Under such circumstances, requiring the children who have been abused or abandoned to submit to the maintenance orders by the Tribunal must appear to be unjustified.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: In speaking with social workers on this issue, I understand from their experiences that the complexity of family relationships is very high.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Many of the parents who are destitute or homeless, either on the streets or in shelters, have been living this way by choice and over a long period of time.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The reason in almost all cases is that they are estranged from their spouse and the children and more often than not, they are the ones who walked out on the family and abandoned the children.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Most of them do not wish to even start the process of conciliation as they do believe that they were the ones at fault and that there is no reason for their children to take them back.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Often, when they go to the social service agencies, they will ask help to get government support for a rental home, shelter, financial aid, but shy away from asking for conciliation.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Moreover, they do not wish to bring the Government into their complicated family matters as they do not see how it could do anything to improve the already estranged relationships.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: There are, of course, also cases whereby unmarried children, the singles, are left supporting their elderly parents even if other siblings can afford to weigh in.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Still, very often, like many of the hon Members who have spoken before me have shared, many of the parents are too shy to put their children in the hands of legislation.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The social workers have seen all these things happen often enough.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Still, in Singapore, we have this law to provide the abandoned elderly a last resort for support, fairly and justly.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I do have a few questions for the hon Member Seah Kian Peng and his team.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: How many cases have been handled since this Bill passed into law in 1995?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Based on the past cases, how many would have been dismissed if the amendments being debated today were taken into consideration?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: From the experiences of the social workers, the elderly who need help would probably approach the social service agencies first and the social workers will always propose conciliatory engagement with the family even as they help the elderly with ComCare or Silver Support where appropriate.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: We did not give ourselves lives but we have received our first great gift of life from our parents.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: As a Catholic, I have been taught from young, "Children, obey your parents for that is what is expected of you.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Honour your father and your mother and it may go well with you and that you may have a long life on the earth." I am sure that my friends of other faiths have similar teachings.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: All the major religions and philosophies of life teach more or less the same thing in this regard.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Children are to honour their parents, which includes actions of care, assistance and support, especially when parents become elderly and/or are not financially independent.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Likewise, parents must fulfil their responsibilities for having brought their children into this world.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: It is sad when such cases occur and are symptoms of deeper issues in society that need to be resolved.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: One's family is the gift we have been given.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: For those who may have been gifted, unfortunately, with a family that has been a "living hell" for them, I can only pray and hope that they may find closure and conciliation.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: It was quite heartening to hear one of the hon Members share a story whereby one of the siblings forgave the parents who were asking for maintenance.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Throughout the ages, captivating tales of filial devotion have been woven into the tapestry of our cultural heritage.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They serve as powerful reminders of the importance of honouring and caring for our parents.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: One of the most famous stories about filial piety comes from the classic teachings of Confucianism, known as the Twenty-Four Filial Exemplars.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: One of the teachings involved a man named Jiang Ge, who lived during the Eastern Han Dynasty.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As a young boy, he lost his father.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: He was brought up by his mother, whom he became extremely devoted to.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: During a period of war and chaos, Jiang Ge fled his hometown, carrying his elderly mother on his back all the way.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But upon witnessing Jiang Ge's filial piety, the bandits could not bear to harm the mother and son, and even pointed out a safe route to him.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Jiang Ge and his mother eventually found safe refuge and he worked hard and lived simply.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This was to ensure that his mother had everything she needed until the end of her days.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Jiang Ge's story is a powerful example of filial piety, where a son's unwavering commitment to his mother's wellbeing in the face of adversity is recognised and honoured, even by crooks.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It also epitomises the very essence of filial piety – the importance of caring for and respecting our parents, regardless of the challenges we may encounter.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It mirrors the sacrifices that parents make to raise their children.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It illustrates the reciprocity inherent in the bond between parents and offspring.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This captivating story, much like others within the Twenty-Four Filial Exemplars, vividly illustrates the ideal relationship between parents and children.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This Bill that we are discussing today ultimately revolves around this concept of filial piety.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Families face a myriad of unique issues, ranging from instances of parental abuse and neglect to cases where the children themselves endure these hardships inflicted on them by their own parents.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is precisely because of these complexities and the need to address such diverse situations that we find ourselves gathered here today.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is important to consider that many of these cases date back to a time when the adult children were themselves young and vulnerable.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It was uncommon for children of that age to speak out or report their parents' actions.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In the past, conflicts within families were typically treated as private affairs.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: These were often resolved or not talked about beyond the household without formal reports.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As a result, access to family counselling was limited.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The idea of foster care or shelters then was also felt to be primarily catered to children who had lost their parents.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is only in recent years where there are more government initiatives to raise awareness that domestic abuse has begun to be taken more seriously.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Considering these circumstances, it raises the question of what additional services or processes are available to assist these individuals in providing evidence of such neglect or abuse.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Without a Police or social welfare report, how else can they substantiate claims of ill treatment?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For instance, let us consider a situation where a child's basic needs were met but he endured frequent verbal abuse or witnessed his mother being subjected to abuse due to their father's infidelity, gambling addiction or alcoholism.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: These circumstances had a profound impact on his upbringing and mental well-being.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In response to this toxic environment, the child made the difficult decision to estrange himself from his family as soon as he was financially capable.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Should this child be expected to resume his responsibility to financially support his parents?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What if the parents' financial hardship is a result of their own financial mismanagement or previous instances of family abuse?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Additionally, how many of these destitute parents have willingly chosen this path despite having the means to provide a roof over their own heads?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Also, in doing so, are we inadvertently perpetuating the notion of children being seen as a retirement plan, a concept that is progressively being questioned by youths today?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Should individuals who have suffered severe abuse at the hands of their parents, to the point where attending mandatory conciliatory sessions would trigger them and reopen old wounds, be forced to participate in these sessions?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Sharing such data can help identify any patterns or discrepancies, enabling us to make informed decisions and address any issues that may arise.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The virtue of honouring parents stands as a golden rule that has been ingrained in various religions and cultures throughout history.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Nevertheless, we have to recognise that complex dynamics interplay within families.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The reality is that no two families are the same and perfection is often elusive.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Each family faces its own unique set of challenges and problems.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: During my interactions with residents at my Meet-the-People Sessions (MPS) in Yio Chu Kang, I have witnessed numerous cases typifying these complex dynamics.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Sibling rivalries and disparities in wealth between the children's families often place a significant strain on the division of caregiving responsibilities for their parents.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is not uncommon for unmarried children to shoulder the primary burden of caregiving for aged parents, leading to feelings of resentment and imbalance.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Furthermore, the introduction of spouses into the equation further complicates matters.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In such distressing cases, the state needs to provide avenues for justice for parents who have selflessly devoted themselves to raising their children.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Responsible parenting plays a significant role in shaping children into model citizens.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Parents should actively engage with their children, spend quality time with them and provide emotional support.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They should be good role models by treating their own parents and their children's grandparents with love and respect.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: By strengthening the bonds between parents and children, we can build a foundation of trust and love within families.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: When love becomes the driving force within families, familial duty comes naturally.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is an intrinsic expression of affection and care, rather than being perceived as a burden or legal obligation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is how we support families in Singapore, by building a resilient society that values family well-being and supports caregiving.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: The MPA, which governs the financial support and maintenance of elderly parents, warrants our attention due to its profound implications on society.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Under the MPA, children who are capable of providing support but neglect their duty to do so can be legally obligated to provide financial maintenance to their parents.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: The MPA recognises the importance of upholding the values of filial piety and social responsibility, which are deeply rooted in the fabric of our society.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: It serves as a means to safeguard the well-being and dignity of elderly parents who may be financially dependent or vulnerable.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: By providing a legal mechanism, the MPA aims to ensure that elderly parents receive the necessary support from their children to meet their basic needs and maintain a reasonable standard of living.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: In a nutshell, the MPA stands as a legislative pillar, reflecting the core values of our society.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: It serves as a poignant reminder of our responsibility that adult children bear towards their ageing parents.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: It encapsulates the cherished belief that filial sons and daughters should provide unwavering care and support during their parents' golden years.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Amidst the ever-evolving nature of our society, we must not allow ourselves to lose sight of the intrinsic values of respect, love and care that permeate our cultural fabric.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: It is incumbent upon us to foster an environment that encourages the nurturing of these values within our communities.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: By doing so, we empower Singaporeans, particularly the Malay/Muslim community, to preserve the sacred tenets of filial piety while adapting to the demands of contemporary life.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Education and awareness programmes must take centrestage, enlightening individuals about the fundamental significance of fulfilling their duties towards their parents.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: These initiatives should delve beyond mere financial obligations and focus on the emotional and psychological aspects of caregiving.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: By fostering understanding and empathy within families, we can facilitate meaningful conversations that bridge generational gaps and strengthen familial bonds.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Furthermore, we can harness the power of community resources, such as counselling services and support networks, to assist individuals facing financial constraints while ensuring their parents' well-being.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: (In Malay):   Addressing destitution as a "last resort" option.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Nonetheless, as we navigate the complexities of caregiving and familial responsibilities, we must acknowledge that exceptional circumstances may arise, leaving families in dire straits.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: These are instances where parents, through no fault of their own, find themselves destitute and without adequate support.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: It is during these moments of profound vulnerability that we, as a compassionate society, must step forward and consider this "last resort".

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: This safety net, designed as a compassionate response, aims to ensure that the basic needs of these vulnerable parents are met.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: It is essential that we approach this option with utmost sensitivity, empathy and an unwavering commitment to maintaining the dignity of those in need.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Collaborative efforts between Government agencies, social service organisations and community leaders are crucial to establishing a robust support system that offers financial assistance, housing, healthcare and social services for destitute parents.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Moreover, as we explore this "last resort" option, we must also emphasise the importance of preventative measures.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: By investing in early intervention programs, financial literacy initiatives and comprehensive social support networks, we can empower families to overcome potential challenges before they reach a critical point.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: These proactive measures can help alleviate the risk of destitution and ensure that families have the necessary resources and knowledge to fulfil their filial duties without resorting to extreme measures.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Furthermore, fostering a culture of compassion and understanding within our communities is essential.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: We must encourage open conversations and eliminate the stigma surrounding financial difficulties and caregiving challenges.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: By providing a supportive environment, we can create avenues for collaboration, shared experiences and the exchange of knowledge and resources.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Together, we can collectively work towards alleviating the burdens faced by families and ensure that destitution remains an absolute last resort.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: By implementing a compassionate "last resort" option and investing in preventative measures, we demonstrate our commitment to upholding our cultural values while safeguarding the well-being of vulnerable parents.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Let us continue to foster a society where no parent is left behind, where the bonds of family are cherished, and where compassion and empathy prevail.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Verily, paradise lies beneath the feet of mothers.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: With strong families, many societal challenges we face today will become much more manageable.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Today, strong values hold us together as a family, as a society.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Upholding these values are important as they underpin our way of thinking and our way of life.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Likewise, for their unmarried children, 82% were able to rely on them for physical support, 91% for emotional support and 83% for financial support in times of need.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: So, clearly, Singaporeans continue to hold the family as a fundamental bulwark of our society – family members caring for and supporting one another.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: It makes us different and it helps us think beyond ourselves.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Some societies regard the individual as supreme and triumphs over the family.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: To be sure, this affirms the dignity of every person and allows individual potential and special talents to flourish.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: But such an individual is likely to also attribute his achievements to his own capability and may not stop to look at his family, his community and society which provided the conditions for his success.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: As each generation feels it had made it solely on its own steam, mutual care and support across generations weaken.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: In Singapore's case, however, we believe that strong families empower its individual members to thrive and to flourish, which is why strong families make for a resilient Singapore society.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: And this will be increasingly crucial as Singapore ages.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Families are, therefore, crucial as the first line of care and support, and taking care of our parents must continue to be the norm.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: The MPA reflects the accepted values of most Singaporeans and upholds what we value as a society.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Recent ForwardSG engagements and these MPA amendments have affirmed that Singaporeans today continue to hold strongly to the principles of "self-reliance" and "family as the first line of support".

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: I agree with Mr Don Wee, Mr Yip Hon Weng and Ms Janet Ang, along with Members of the Workgroup, on the need for more upstream efforts.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: We are strengthening the Families for Life movement, which aims to inculcate family values, working with schools and community partners, as well as to promote family bonding, including across generations.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Values education starts at home and I hope parents will also role model the type of families that we want our next generations to have.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: That said, legislation is still important and relevant.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: The MPA is meant to be applied for a small minority of children who neglect their responsibility when their parents cannot support themselves adequately, and they have the means to help.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: In 2022, slightly over 100 elderly parents sought a maintenance order under the MPA.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Most of them managed to resolve their maintenance disputes with their children at conciliation.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Only a very small number proceeded to bring their dispute to the Tribunal.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Yet, one is one too many, and there is room for improvement.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Mr Don Wee raised a point on the sharing of responsibility so that no child is overwhelmed by the financial obligation of supporting his parents alone.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: For the elderly and families who do not have enough financial resources, the community and the state will step up to play a bigger role.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: We are invested in supporting and strengthening families and will continue to help lower-income elderly who do not have family support, or whose children lack the means to support them.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: This includes support schemes such as: (a)	the Pioneer Generation Package, which provides healthcare benefits for life for all Singapore Citizens born before 1950; (b) the Silver Support Scheme, which provides quarterly cash supplements to Singaporeans who had low incomes throughout life and who have little or no family support in old age; (c) ComCare, which supports lower-income households with their basic living needs; (d) the Community Network for Seniors, which involves Government agencies and community partners teaming up to reach out to seniors, especially those who are lower-income or living alone, to help them stay active, socially engaged and connected to support and health services; as well as (e) the Senior Mobility and Enabling Fund, which provides subsidies for assistive devices, transport and home healthcare items for seniors to age in place within the community.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: At the same time, there is support for families to care for their elderly members.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: As part of Singapore Made for Families, there will be more caregiver support, such as respite services and enhanced Home Caregiving Grant, as well as counselling and mediation support.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: MSF supports the thrust of the amendments raised by the Workgroup, which seeks to enhance the powers of the Tribunal and the Commissioner in ensuring neglected elderly parents are adequately supported.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: At the same time, safeguards in the MPA will be strengthened to prevent its misuse by those who did not fulfil their parental duties.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: The amendments are very much in line with the spirit and intent of the MPA and build upon previous work to make the legislation even more fit for its purpose.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: At this juncture, I wish to give a more detailed response to some of the key amendments.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: First, on the power of the Commissioner concerning destitute parents.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: The MPA provides a last resort to compel maintenance from children who neglect their duty towards their elderly parents.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: But as the Workgroup rightly pointed out, it is of no use if the parent refuses to initiate the process.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: We know of a few destitute parents residing in state-funded welfare homes who had children they could have relied on in their old age.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: But the children exploited their parents' reluctance to file a claim and shunned their responsibility when they clearly have the means to maintain their parents.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: The many attempts to persuade the children were futile.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng has asked how many destitute parents have willingly chosen this path despite having the means to provide a roof over their own heads.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: To clarify, people who have the means to provide a roof over their heads would not meet the criteria for being destitute under the Destitute Persons Act.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Only those who are unable to support themselves and lack family support can be admitted into welfare homes.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Some may think this is an attempt to transfer the burden of caring for our needy elderly from the state onto the children.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: So, only a small number would meet the threshold for intervention.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: For the few that do, it is important that the Commissioner can call the children down for conciliation and discuss their parent's care.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: My next point is on the making of non-monetary directions.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Our families have remained strong, but they are also getting smaller and seeing their resources stretched with fewer working members supporting the young and the old.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Gambling addiction is another reason cited by the children refusing to maintain their parent.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: To resolve maintenance disputes in such cases, we need to address this root cause.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: My Ministry works with the National Council on Problem Gambling to adopt a multi-pronged approach in tackling problem gambling.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Specifically, we have implemented preventive measures through public education and to encourage problem gamblers to seek help.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: We also have social safeguards, such as "the exclusion and visit limit" regime, to mitigate the problem.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: The Workgroup's amendment here further complements the Council's work in nudging problem gamblers to seek help.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Lastly, the Workgroup also proposes to protect survivors of abuse from being put through unnecessary distress and painful memories, often triggered when they had to face their parent who abused them.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: We have just had an extensive debate on the Family Violence Amendment Bill.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: That Bill touched on how survivors are empowered to better protect themselves, the Government's ability to intervene in family violence cases, and empowering the Court to make additional rehabilitative orders, raise penalties and strengthen enforcement against breaches.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: This Bill, on the other hand, deals with the long-lasting effects of childhood abuse, which can linger on for many years.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Perpetrators can cause direct harm to their family members through physical or emotional abuse and harassment, but they can also cause indirect harm by using institutions and legal processes.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Effects of childhood abuse can be long-lasting, and research has shown that the effects of exposure to reminders of the past abuse can sometimes be as bad as when it first happened.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: This young woman experienced emotional and physical abuse by her mother and stepfather since she was very young.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: She was told that she was useless and had things – physical objects – thrown at her.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: When she was not even 10 years old, her stepfather started to sexually abuse her, and MSF was alerted of her case a few years later.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: After receiving therapy, I am glad to note that she was able to complete her Polytechnic education and find employment in life.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: However, the long-term effects of abuse are still manifest in her daily life, such as her fear of loud noises, low self-esteem and, occasionally, self-harm and suicidal tendencies.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Till today, communication with her mother often evokes strong reactions, such as feelings of fear and anxiety.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: For families and individuals who have experienced abuse or violence, my Ministry will continue to strengthen protection and provide support for these survivors.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Where there are records, these survivors will no longer be retraumatised by their perpetrator through the MPA.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: This amendment thus builds on our efforts in this area.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: But where that is not enough, the family stands as a key pillar of support.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Maybe before I start my speech, I just want to respond very quickly —

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: In relation to what Mr Louis Ng said about his case theory – I had read his speech which he left on his chair while he was away – I think Mr Ng may have overrated my ability to speedread his speech and write a 12-page speech which I delivered just moments ago.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: But I will take some credit for being prescient enough to have noted some of the points that he wanted to raise in his speech.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The hon Member, Mr Louis Ng, argued for the child to participate in the proceedings initiated by the parents who have had records of abandonment, neglect or abuse (ANA), to get permission to apply for maintenance from their children.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: He pointed out that the child may wish to have the opportunity to decide whether or not to participate in the application for permission.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: He also wondered how the Tribunal would be able to determine if there is a good arguable case to grant permission without the child's involvement since he or she would have been a victim of the parents' abandonment, neglect or abuse.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: He further postulated that it may be traumatic for a child who was not involved in the permission application to be, quoting his words, "suddenly told that they face a maintenance application", as the Commissioner or Tribunal found that there was no abandonment, neglect or abuse, without hearing the child.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: In response to the hon Member, it may be useful to remind ourselves about the starting point today under the Act.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Under the Act today, where a parent commences an application against his child for maintenance, the child is drawn in immediately.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: There is no prior screening conducted against the parent to establish if he had a record of abandonment, neglect or abuse of the child.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The child will have to undergo a compulsory conciliation process before the matter heads to the Tribunal.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The conciliation process alone can take – off the top of my head – about six months.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Should the case not settle at conciliation, it is then referred to the Tribunal.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: At the hearing before the Tribunal, the child may give evidence of his or her parent's abandonment, neglect or abuse (ANA), which the Tribunal is bound to consider before making a decision on whether it is just and equitable to order that the child pays maintenance to the parent.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The professionals who deal with family violence cases also told us that children in such circumstances would probably suffer from significant emotional pain triggered by past events involving their parents.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: It is a point that was echoed by several Members who spoke in favour of this amendments just now.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Where the parent is established to have an official record of ANA, it is not as crucial to have the child's involvement to enable the Tribunal to make a decision whether permission ought to be given.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The hon Member Mr Ng asked what is required evidentially to show a "good arguable case".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I wish to also add that, ordinarily, the records should speak for themselves.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Contrary to what the hon Member suggested, there should not be too much subjectivity involved when it comes to perusing and understanding the contents of the records.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Furthermore, the Tribunal consists of persons with a wealth of experience.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The President and Deputy President of the Tribunal, who heads each Tribunal, have the qualifications of a District Judge.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The Tribunal is well equipped to make evidential assessments and determine in each case whether the parent has discharged his burden.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The hon Member may then ask why give the parent who has an official record of ANA the right to ask for permission to apply for maintenance from his child.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The reason is really to ensure fairness and justice for the parent.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: He should, for example, be allowed to argue that the document providing details of his case does not objectively suggest that he has a record of ANA or that it does not present a full and accurate picture.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The hon Member invited me to provide guides, some guidance to the Tribunal on how it should proceed with its duties in assessing whether or not to grant permission.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I mentioned that the Tribunal consists of experienced people who are more than qualified to make determinations without such assistance.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: In fact, the policy objective is quite the opposite.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: To give the Tribunal wide latitude to determine what is just and equitable having regard to the circumstances of the case.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: As was mentioned during my speech earlier, there is one narrow exception to the rule of not involving the child – where the Commissioner learns about the parent having a record of ANA during conciliation proceedings with the child.

speaker: Mdm Deputy Speaker
text: Mr Murali, can you keep it brief, please.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I would, therefore, not characterise the proposal in the Bill to provide for a sieving mechanism that I described as making it more traumatising for the child as suggested by the hon Member.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: It is noteworthy that, by this point, the parents with official records of ANA would have been excluded unless they obtain permission from the Tribunal.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: We would have succeeded in protecting the children of these parents from being re-traumatised.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The hon Member asked if the child may challenge the Tribunal's decision to grant the parent permission to proceed with the application to apply for maintenance.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The child's rights as they exist under the Act today are preserved.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: He asked what recourse does a child who is affected by this have.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The Tribunal will be able to accord appropriate weight to such evidence and decide in accordance with what is just and equitable in the circumstances.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: And I apologise if I almost outstayed your welcome.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: My sincere thanks to all who have spoken.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: At this point, a lot of key comments and questions have been dealt with and in these closing remarks, I hope to reiterate why the proposed amendments are needed.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: But first, let me thank my workgroup members comprising Ms Tin Pei Ling, Mr Murali Pillai, Ms Denise Phua, Ms Carrie Tan, Ms Ng Ling Ling, Ms Joan Pereira, Mr Fahmi Aliman and Mr Melvin Yong.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: All of them have played an important part in putting together this Bill.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: We did not initially agree on everything, and many of the issues discussed today had also been debated internally.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: I also want to thank all of them for speaking in this debate today to further explain the different perspectives, articulate their own views and how we eventually landed on these recommendations in this amendment Bill.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: There were also many others who journeyed with us over the last one-and-a-half years as we deliberated, as we listened in to the focus groups, as we analysed the surveys, as we talked to various stakeholders – and the list goes on.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: This piece of legislative work is very much a result of their efforts for which I am eternally grateful to all of them.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
